intro: The finale of the New World Symphony opens with rushing strings and a brass tune built to fill a hall. By the end, melodies from all four movements have returned, and the last E-major chord fades in the winds after the strings have stopped.

sections.label: A · Strings rush towards the brass
sections.mNote: Rising string figures launch the broad brass tune

sections.label: B · A clarinet song in G major
sections.mNote: The clarinet sings while cellos weave quick figures below

sections.label: Dev · Earlier tunes return
sections.mNote: The Largo and scherzo meet the finale’s own melody

sections.label: A′ · The main tune returns
sections.mNote: The opening tune leads a shortened return of earlier music

sections.label: Coda · Brass recalls the Largo chords
sections.mNote: The slow movement’s chords return in the full orchestra

sections.label: Link · Clarinets above a held bass
sections.mNote: The orchestra softens to give the winds room

sections.label: Close · E major and a fading chord
sections.mNote: The final chord remains in the winds after the strings stop

cues.title: Strings before the brass
cues.text: The strings begin alone, driving a short figure upwards. Winds and brass enter as the climb reaches its summit. The main tune then strides out in the brass, with a broad opening and a sharply accented answer.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, movement IV, printed pp. 133–137, Allegro con fuoco. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The clarinet takes its time
cues.text: A solo clarinet introduces the second tune in G major. Its long notes float above the cellos’ quick, curling figures. The brass falls silent, and the flutes later join the clarinet’s song.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 146–148: solo clarinet, moving cellos and subsequent flute entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A telegram after the ending
cues.text: On 24 May 1893, Dvořák finishes the score at nine in the morning. That afternoon a telegram tells him his children have reached Southampton on their way to America. He adds the news beside the time of completion.
cues.evidence: Josef Kovařík’s memoir records the completion time and telegram annotation on 24 May 1893; reproduced at https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: The other movements return
cues.text: The development draws on the whole symphony. The Largo’s song and the scherzo’s quick figures meet the finale’s main tune. Dvořák changes their companions and their accompaniment, letting melodies from different movements occupy the same bars.
cues.evidence: The Dvořák work catalogue identifies the combination of themes from movements II, III and IV in the finale’s development: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/. Šourek full score, printed pp. 157–170.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The main tune comes back
cues.text: The finale’s main tune returns after the tangle of earlier melodies. Its broad statement now leads into a shortened recapitulation. Dvořák saves the longest reckoning with the symphony’s past for the coda.
cues.evidence: The abbreviated recapitulation and expanded coda are described in the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A title added in November
cues.text: In November 1893, Anton Seidl asks for the score to prepare its première. Just before Kovařík carries it away, Dvořák adds From the New World to the title page. Until that evening, it has simply said Symphony in E minor.
cues.evidence: Josef Kovařík’s memoir places the title-page addition in mid-November 1893, just before he delivered the score to Seidl; reproduced at https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: The Largo’s chords grow immense
cues.text: The coda gathers the symphony’s old tunes around the finale’s own. Even the quiet chords that opened the Largo return, enlarged for the full orchestra. Rising strings press against their long brass notes.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, coda, printed pp. 190–197; the Largo-chord reminiscence is identified in the Dvořák work catalogue.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinets above the quiet bass
cues.text: The orchestra draws back from its huge chords. Repeated string figures soften, and the bass settles into a long note. Clarinets emerge into the space, beginning another quiet recollection before the final climb.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 198–199, bars 310 onwards: diminuendo, held bass and clarinet soli.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The winds keep the ending
cues.text: The closing pages drive towards E major. At the very end, strings, trombones and timpani cut their last chord short, but the other winds and brass hold on. Their sound diminishes to ppp under a long fermata.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 200–204, particularly the final bar: short string, trombone and timpani notes against sustained wind, horn and trumpet notes, diminuendo to ppp and lunga corona.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The brass yields to a clarinet
transitions.from: A · Strings rush towards the brass
transitions.to: B · A clarinet song in G major
transitions.how: The brass withdraws and the strings soften. A solo clarinet opens the G-major second tune, stretching its phrases above the cellos’ quick figures. The upper strings hold long chords while the melody finds room to breathe.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 146–148, lyrical second subject.

transitions.title: The strings reopen the argument
transitions.from: B · A clarinet song in G major
transitions.how: The exposition’s closing figures diminish over a held bass. The first violins turn upwards from this quiet ending, setting the development in motion. Horns, trumpets and winds take up memories of the other movements above the moving strings.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 156–160: diminished closing figures, rising violin phrase and ensuing development.

transitions.title: The main tune gathers the orchestra
transitions.how: Repeated wind chords and rising violin figures build towards the main tune’s return. Horns, bassoons and low strings give it weight below the high winds. The returning music follows a shorter course than the exposition, leaving the great accumulation for the coda.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 170–172, rehearsal 8. The shorter recapitulation is described in the Dvořák work catalogue.

transitions.title: The orchestra enlarges the Largo chords
transitions.to: Coda · Brass recalls the Largo chords
transitions.how: At Tempo I, the quieter return gives way to long orchestral chords and a forceful line in bassoons, cellos and basses. The coda gathers earlier themes, including the Largo’s opening chord sequence. Brass sustains the harmony while the strings repeatedly climb beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 190–197, Tempo I and the coda; the Largo-chord return is identified in the Dvořák work catalogue.

transitions.title: The clarinets emerge from the chords
transitions.from: Coda · Brass recalls the Largo chords
transitions.to: Link · Clarinets above a held bass
transitions.how: The wind chords and repeated string figures diminish together. Cellos and basses stop their running notes and hold a quiet foundation. Clarinets begin a new phrase above it, while the brass rests and the timpani roll fades.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 198–199, bars 310 onwards.

transitions.title: E major fills the closing pages
transitions.from: Link · Clarinets above a held bass
transitions.to: Close · E major and a fading chord
transitions.how: The quiet wind recollection grows into the final orchestral drive. Rising strings, emphatic brass and timpani push towards E major. The last chord separates the orchestra: strings, trombones and timpani stop short; winds, horns and trumpets sustain and diminish to ppp.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 200–204, concluding build and final chord.

source.title: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, full score, critical edition edited by Otakar Šourek
source.locator: Movement IV, printed pp. 133–204: rising strings and the brass main tune, lyrical clarinet, returning themes and final E-major chord. Cymbals sound once, held across bars 64–66 on printed p. 146. There is no tuba part.

timeline.note: The strings begin alone, driving a short figure upwards towards the brass entrance.
Horns and trumpets project the broad E-minor tune above moving strings.
A single soft cymbal stroke rings across three bars as the music approaches the clarinet’s song.
The clarinet sings in G major above quick cello figures and held upper strings.
Themes from the Largo and scherzo pass through winds and brass above the moving strings.
The main tune returns across the orchestra before the quieter woodwind phrases.
Oboes and horns hand their phrases to clarinets, above quiet trombone chords, timpani and strings.
The clarinet recovers the lyrical tune, with the other winds and strings answering around it.
Flutes and strings broaden the song, then soften over quiet timpani and held chords.
Brass and timpani rejoin the winds and strings as the coda gathers the symphony’s earlier tunes.
Clarinets sing above a held bass; the horn call follows, with quiet timpani and trombone chords.
The orchestra drives towards E major; winds, horns and trumpets hold the final chord after the strings stop.

composer.epithet: He had played viola in the opera pit for nine years before the world discovered the composer of the Slavonic Dances.
facts: Violist at Prague’s Provisional Theatre, 1862–71; organist and piano teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of New York’s National Conservatory, 1892–95
Nine symphonies; operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs
composer.background:
In the village band at Nelahozeves, north of Prague, the musicians collected their money by stopping a couple halfway through a dance and asking them to pay. Young Antonín Dvořák handed his share straight to his father, the village butcher and innkeeper. “I belonged to ours as soon as I could fiddle a little,” he told the London Sunday Times on 10 May 1885. He had been born there on 8 September 1841.

At Zlonice, the schoolteacher Antonín Liehmann taught him harmony and several instruments. Dvořák remembered bringing home a polka for the band to try: the opening chord came out all right, except for the cornet, whose part he had written in the wrong key. In 1857 he went to the Prague Organ School, graduating two years later. He played viola in a dance band which became the nucleus of the Provisional Theatre orchestra in 1862. For nine years he sat in the pit, often under Smetana, playing operas while writing his own music at home.
